# Enterobacterales

> *Most people carry one species of Gram-negative rod in the colon all their lives without harm, yet
> strains of the same species cause bladder infection, bloody diarrhoea and meningitis in the first
> weeks of life. A small set of extra genes, and the site the bacteria reach, separate the dangerous
> strains from the harmless residents.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Describe the traits the Enterobacterales share, and explain how lactose fermentation on MacConkey
  agar sorts them in the laboratory.
- Explain how extra genes for pili, toxins and a capsule let some strains of *Escherichia coli*, a
  resident of the colon, cause urinary tract infection, diarrhoea, kidney failure and meningitis in
  neonates.
- Explain how its capsule and acquired resistance make *Klebsiella pneumoniae* a cause of hospital
  infection, and how strains with an extra-thick capsule cause liver abscess outside hospital.
- Explain how survival inside macrophages lets *Salmonella* Typhi spread from the gut to the blood,
  and why carriers keep typhoid in circulation.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main organism cause disease.
- Tell *Salmonella* from *Shigella* by infectious dose, reservoir, site of disease and toxin.
:::

## The group {#sec-ent-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-ent-sentence}

The Enterobacterales are Gram-negative rods that grow with or without oxygen, ferment sugars and, in
many cases, live in the gut of humans and animals, and whether one of them causes disease depends
largely on the extra genes it carries and the site it reaches. Most of the six questions have one
answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in those extra genes.

The name is that of a taxonomic order (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-names)).
Older sources and some laboratory reports call the group the Enterobacteriaceae, now the name of one
family within the order.

| Question | Answer for the Enterobacterales |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A Gram-negative envelope: thin peptidoglycan under an outer membrane whose lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is endotoxin; most members have flagella and **pili**, short, hair-like protein fibres that attach a bacterium to surfaces, and some a **capsule**, a polysaccharide layer outside the cell wall that resists phagocytosis (see [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)) |
| How does it get energy? | Facultative anaerobe: respires with oxygen and ferments sugars without it, so it grows overnight on ordinary media; nearly all members are oxidase negative, lacking the respiratory enzyme that the oxidase test detects (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-habitat)) |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission, as often as every 20 minutes in good conditions; acquires genes for virulence and for drug resistance on plasmids, phages and pathogenicity islands, and passes them between species |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | The gut of humans and animals; spread by the faecal–oral route in food and water, and on hands, including between patients in hospital; some members live only in humans |
| How does damage happen? | Endotoxin in the blood drives inflammation and shock; beyond that, each organism has its own tools: pili, toxins, a capsule, or survival inside cells |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall and the enzymes that build it, the targets of the drugs most used against the group |

Every member carries endotoxin in its outer membrane (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope)). When the bacteria multiply in the blood,
endotoxin drives widespread inflammation with dilated, leaky vessels, and the resulting
**hypotension**, abnormally low blood pressure, can progress to shock (see [*How bacteria cause
damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-endotoxin)). *E. coli* and *Klebsiella* are the commonest
Gram-negative causes of bloodstream infection, which usually begins in an infected urinary tract,
abdomen or lung.

The members also share genes. In the gut, *E. coli*, *Klebsiella* and their relatives live side by
side, and plasmids pass between them by conjugation (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-hgt)). A gene for resistance that one species acquires can
therefore appear in another, so resistance in one member soon becomes a problem for the whole group.

### Sorting the group {#sec-ent-key}

All members ferment glucose, but only some ferment lactose. The laboratory reads the difference on
**MacConkey agar**, a medium containing bile salts, which suppress most Gram-positive bacteria, and
lactose with a dye that turns pink in acid. Gut bacteria tolerate bile, so they grow on it, and the
acid made by lactose fermenters turns their colonies pink. MacConkey agar is therefore both a
selective and a differential medium (see [*Detecting bacteria and testing
susceptibility*](detecting-bacteria.qmd#sec-dbac-culture)).

Lactose fermentation says little about how an organism causes disease, but it helps the laboratory
find pathogens among the residents. Most *E. coli* ferment lactose, so a stool sample gives many pink
colonies, and the pale colonies of *Salmonella* and *Shigella*, which do not ferment lactose, stand
out among them. Beyond the colour of the colony, we sort the members by the traits that let them
cause disease, because those traits also predict where the disease occurs.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the Enterobacterales]{.tree-title}

- Ferment lactose: pink colonies on MacConkey agar
  - Flagella; strains differ in extra genes for pili, toxins and a capsule: *E. coli*
  - A thick capsule and no flagella: *K. pneumoniae*
- Do not ferment lactose: pale colonies
  - Survives inside macrophages: *Salmonella*
  - Invades the lining of the colon, and a few bacteria are enough: *Shigella*
  - Splits urea and infects the urinary tract: *Proteus mirabilis*
  - Grows in chilled food and infects the gut: *Yersinia enterocolitica*
:::

What a member carries predicts where it causes disease and who is most at risk:

| What it carries | Where it causes disease | Who is most at risk |
|---|---|---|
| Pili that hold the bacteria on the lining of the bladder and, in strains with extra genes, the kidney (*E. coli*) | The bladder and, if the bacteria climb further, the kidney | Women, whose urethra is short; people with a urinary catheter |
| Toxins that act on the gut (some *E. coli*; *Shigella dysenteriae* type 1) | The gut; one of these toxins also damages the kidney | Travellers and young children who swallow food or water contaminated with faeces |
| A thick capsule (*K. pneumoniae*; some *E. coli*) | The lungs, the urinary tract and the blood, where the capsule resists phagocytes | Hospital patients with breathing tubes, catheters or weakened defences |
| Survival inside macrophages (*Salmonella*) | The lining of the gut; for *Salmonella* Typhi, the lymph nodes, liver, spleen and blood | Anyone who swallows enough bacteria; *S.* Typhi spreads beyond the gut in healthy people, other *Salmonella* mainly in infants, older adults and people with weakened defences |
| Invasion of the lining of the colon (*Shigella*) | The colon, where it causes **dysentery**, diarrhoea with blood in the stool | Young children, and anyone in close contact with a patient |

Work through the key from the colour of the colonies, and read at each branch what the trait
predicts about the organism.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/ent-key.yml"></div>

## Main organisms {#sec-ent-main}

### *Escherichia coli*: residents and strains with extra genes {#sec-ent-ecoli}

*E. coli*, one of the anchor organisms (see [*The microbial
world*](../foundations/microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-anchors)), colonises the gut in the first days
of life and stays in the colon of most people for life. It is the commonest facultative anaerobe
there, respiring with oxygen and fermenting without it, although obligate anaerobes such as
*Bacteroides fragilis* outnumber it many times over (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-body)).

Most resident strains are **commensals**, organisms that live on a host without harming it. Strains
that cause disease carry extra genes that the residents lack, acquired by gene transfer: on plasmids,
in prophages built into the chromosome, or in pathogenicity islands, clusters of virulence genes
acquired together (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-hgt)). Each set of extra genes suits a strain to a particular
site in the body, and the site decides the disease.

Disease-causing strains come from inside or outside the body. Strains that cause urinary tract and
bloodstream infection come from the person's own gut, so these are **endogenous infections**,
infections caused by an organism the person already carries. A **neonate**, a newborn infant in the
first four weeks of life, acquires its first *E. coli* from the mother during birth, and with it any
strain able to invade its blood. Strains that cause diarrhoea come from outside, swallowed in food or water
contaminated with faeces (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)).

A **urinary tract infection** is an infection of the bladder (**cystitis**) or of the kidney
(**pyelonephritis**), and *E. coli* is its commonest cause. Bacteria from the gut reach the skin
around the opening of the urethra and climb the urethra into the bladder. The female urethra is
short, so women are infected far more often than men, and a urinary catheter gives bacteria a path
in either sex. The flow of urine washes out bacteria that cannot hold on. Most *E. coli* have pili
tipped with **adhesins**, bacterial surface molecules that bind a specific molecule on a host cell or
in the tissue around it, and these adhesins bind the cells lining the bladder (see [*How bacteria
cause damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-attach)). Strains that cause urinary infection carry
extra genes as well, among them genes for further pili whose adhesins bind the lining of the upper
urinary tract and kidney, which favours pyelonephritis.

Strains that cause diarrhoea carry genes for toxins. Some attach to the lining of the small intestine
and release **enterotoxins**, toxins that act on the gut, which make its cells secrete salt and
water; the bacteria do not invade, and the diarrhoea is watery. Others carry a prophage encoding
**Shiga toxin**, a toxin that enters cells and stops them making protein, which kills them, together
with a pathogenicity island for attaching tightly to the lining of the colon (see [*How bacteria copy
themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-phage)). Cattle carry these strains in the
gut without illness, and people are infected from undercooked minced beef, unpasteurised milk and
vegetables contaminated with cattle faeces, and then from one another, because a small number of
bacteria is enough.

Shiga toxin kills cells of the colon lining and of the small blood vessels in its wall, so the
diarrhoea becomes bloody. The toxin, without the bacteria, then enters the blood and damages the
lining of small vessels elsewhere, above all in the kidney. In a minority of patients, most often
young children, the result is **haemolytic uraemic syndrome**: destruction of red blood cells, a fall
in platelets, and kidney failure, as the damaged small vessels fill with clots. Antibacterial drugs
are generally avoided when Shiga-toxin-producing *E. coli* is suspected, because they may increase
the release of toxin and the risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome; care is supportive.

A neonate's immature defences may fail to contain the strains it meets at birth. **Meningitis** is
inflammation of the meninges, the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord. Most of the strains
that cause it in neonates share one kind of polysaccharide capsule, which protects them in the blood
until they cross into the meninges. *E. coli* and group B streptococcus are the two commonest causes
of meningitis in neonates (see [*Gram-positive cocci*](gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-supporting)).

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Urinary tract infection | Strains from the person's own gut climb the urethra; pili hold them on the bladder lining against the flow of urine | Cystitis in a young woman, with pain on passing urine and frequent urination; pyelonephritis, with fever and pain in the loin, if the bacteria climb to the kidney |
| Watery diarrhoea | Swallowed strains attach to the lining of the small intestine and release enterotoxins, which make its cells secrete salt and water; the bacteria do not invade | Travellers' diarrhoea, a few days after arriving where sanitation is poor |
| Bloody diarrhoea and kidney failure | Strains from cattle attach to the lining of the colon and release Shiga toxin, which kills cells of the lining and of small vessels; the toxin reaches the kidney in the blood | Bloody diarrhoea in a young child after a barbecue, followed a week later by haemolytic uraemic syndrome |
| Meningitis in a neonate | Strains with a particular capsule, met at birth, survive in the blood and cross into the meninges | Meningitis in a neonate, with bacteria in the blood as well |
| Bloodstream infection | Bacteria from an infected urinary tract or abdomen enter the blood, where endotoxin drives inflammation that can cause shock | **Bacteraemia**, bacteria in the bloodstream, with fever and hypotension in an older adult with pyelonephritis |

*E. coli* also shows how resistance spreads in the group. Many of the drugs used against the group
are **beta-lactams**, a family of drugs, named for the ring of atoms at their core, that block the
building of the peptidoglycan wall; the family includes the penicillins, the cephalosporins and the
carbapenems. A **beta-lactamase** is an enzyme that breaks down beta-lactams by opening that ring.
Many strains of *E. coli* have acquired an **extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)**, a
beta-lactamase that destroys most penicillins and cephalosporins but not carbapenems. ESBL genes are
carried on plasmids, so they spread between strains and species in the gut (see [*How bacteria copy
themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mechanisms)). A person can carry an
ESBL-producing strain in the gut without symptoms, and when that strain later causes a urinary or
bloodstream infection, the penicillins and cephalosporins usually used no longer work; the same
plasmids often carry genes for resistance to other drug classes as well. Infections with these
strains are often treated with carbapenems, and that use in turn selects bacteria that make a
**carbapenemase**, a beta-lactamase that also destroys carbapenems
(see [*K. pneumoniae*](#sec-ent-klebsiella)).

Three conditions let *E. coli* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | For urinary infection, a woman, or anyone with a urinary catheter; for diarrhoea, a traveller or a young child; for meningitis, a neonate | The short female urethra and a catheter give gut bacteria a path to the bladder; travellers and young children swallow food or water contaminated with faeces where sanitation is poor; a neonate's defences are immature |
| Where (setting) | The person's own gut; for diarrhoeal strains, food or water contaminated with human or cattle faeces | Strains with the extra genes for urinary infection already live in the colon; diarrhoeal strains are swallowed |
| How (route) | Up the urethra to the bladder; swallowed into the gut; from the mother at birth into a neonate's blood | Pili hold the bacteria on the bladder lining; toxins act on the gut and, for Shiga toxin, the kidney; a capsule protects the bacteria in the blood |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is *E. coli* a food-poisoning bacterium?
News reports of outbreaks and food recalls name *E. coli* so often that the bacterium is commonly
equated with food poisoning. Most *E. coli* are commensals of the healthy gut, and the outbreaks are
caused by a few strains with extra genes, such as those that make Shiga toxin. Drinking water and
food are tested for *E. coli* because it lives in the gut of people and other warm-blooded animals
and is easy to grow. Finding it shows that faeces have reached the water or food, and with them any
pathogens the faeces carry.
:::

Step through the two routes *E. coli* takes: from the gut to the bladder and the blood, and from
cattle to the colon and the kidney.

### *Klebsiella pneumoniae*: the capsule and acquired resistance {#sec-ent-klebsiella}

*K. pneumoniae* lives in the gut, and sometimes the throat, of some healthy people, and in water and
soil. It has no flagella and is wrapped in a thick capsule, which makes its colonies large,
wet-looking and sticky. In a healthy person it seldom causes disease. Outside hospital it can cause
severe pneumonia in people with alcohol dependence or diabetes, the disease that gave the species its
name. In hospital it is one of the commonest causes of **healthcare-associated infection**, infection
acquired in the course of medical care. Patients given antibacterial drugs lose part of their
resident microbiota and are colonised by it more often (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-microbiota)), and it passes between patients on the
hands of staff and on shared equipment. Its main targets are the lungs of
patients on a ventilator, the bladder of patients with a urinary catheter, and the blood.

*K. pneumoniae* resists some penicillins from the start, because every strain carries a
beta-lactamase gene on its chromosome. This is **intrinsic resistance**, resistance that is a
property of a whole species. On top of it, *K. pneumoniae* acquires plasmids carrying ESBL and
carbapenemase genes, and passes them to *E. coli* and other members of the group. Carbapenem-resistant
strains have spread through hospitals in many countries, leaving few drugs that still act on them.
Their spread is limited by hand hygiene, by finding and isolating the patients who carry them, and by
careful use of antibacterial drugs (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-stewardship)).

A second kind of *K. pneumoniae* causes disease outside hospital, in people with no device. These
strains are **hypervirulent**, able to cause severe, invasive disease in healthy people, unlike most
strains of the species. They carry extra genes, many of them on one plasmid, that make an extra-thick
capsule and molecules that capture iron from host proteins. They cause a liver abscess, and are
thought to reach the liver from the gut, in the portal vein. From the abscess,
bacteria enter the blood and can settle in the lungs, the meninges or the eye, where they cause
**endophthalmitis**, infection inside the eye, which can destroy sight. In East and South-East Asia,
including Singapore, *K. pneumoniae* is the commonest cause of liver abscess caused by bacteria. Many
patients have diabetes, which impairs neutrophil function (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)), but the infection also occurs in people
with no underlying disease.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Hospital pneumonia | Bacteria from the throat pass along a breathing tube into the lungs; the capsule resists phagocytes in the alveoli | Pneumonia in a patient on a ventilator in intensive care |
| Urinary and bloodstream infection | Bacteria travel along a urinary catheter to the bladder, and from an infected site into the blood, where endotoxin drives shock | Bacteraemia from a carbapenem-resistant strain in a patient with a long-term urinary catheter |
| Liver abscess and spread from it | Hypervirulent strains reach the liver, probably from the gut; the extra-thick capsule resists phagocytes, and bacteria seed the blood | A liver abscess in a man with diabetes in Singapore, followed by endophthalmitis |

Three conditions let *K. pneumoniae* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A hospital patient with a breathing tube, a urinary catheter or weakened defences; for hypervirulent strains, an adult in East or South-East Asia, often with diabetes | Tubes and catheters bypass the barriers that keep bacteria out; the extra-thick capsule protects hypervirulent strains even when defences are intact, and diabetes impairs neutrophils |
| Where (setting) | Hospitals, especially intensive care units; for hypervirulent strains, the community | Antibacterial drugs reduce the resident microbiota, so patients are colonised; hands and equipment carry it between patients |
| How (route) | From the throat along a breathing tube to the lungs; along a catheter to the bladder; for hypervirulent strains, from the gut to the liver | The capsule resists phagocytes wherever the bacteria arrive |

Step through the two routes *K. pneumoniae* takes: in a hospital patient, and from the gut to the
liver and the eye.

### *Salmonella*: survival inside macrophages {#sec-ent-salmonella}

*Salmonella* has flagella and does not ferment lactose, and it is divided into many **serotypes**,
variants distinguished by their surface antigens, here those of the LPS and the flagella. It injects
proteins into the cells lining the gut that make them engulf it. Macrophages that engulf it fail to
kill it, and it survives and multiplies inside them (see [*How bacteria cause
damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-evade)). *Salmonella* is therefore a **facultative
intracellular** bacterium, able to live both inside and outside host cells, unlike most members of
the group, which grow outside them (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-where)).
What follows depends on the serotype.

One serotype, *S.* Typhi, spreads from the gut through the whole body and causes typhoid. Most of the
others are grouped as non-typhoidal *Salmonella*. They live in the gut of poultry, cattle, pigs and
reptiles, so infection with them is a **zoonosis**, an infection transmitted from animals to humans
(see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)). People are infected from
undercooked poultry, eggs and meat, from unpasteurised milk, and from other food contaminated by these
in the kitchen. Stomach acid kills many of the bacteria swallowed, so infection usually needs a large
**inoculum**, the number of organisms received (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)); the bacteria reach such numbers when
contaminated food is left warm. They invade the lining of the end of the small intestine and the
colon, and the inflammation they provoke causes **gastroenteritis**, inflammation of the stomach and
intestines that causes vomiting, diarrhoea or both, here mainly diarrhoea, with fever and abdominal
cramps. It usually begins a day or two after the meal and settles within a week, although the
bacteria are shed in the faeces for some weeks. In infants, older adults and people with weakened
defences, the bacteria can enter the blood.

*S.* Typhi lives only in humans. It spreads in food or water contaminated with the faeces of a
patient or of a **carrier**, a person who harbours and can transmit an organism without being ill, so
it is common where sanitation and water treatment are poor, notably in South Asia, and travellers
acquire it there. *S.* Typhi crosses the lining of the small intestine with little inflammation,
often over the patches of lymphoid tissue in its wall (Peyer's patches).
Macrophages engulf it, but it survives and multiplies inside them, and they carry it to the lymph
nodes that drain the gut and then, in the blood, to the liver, the spleen and the bone marrow, organs
rich in macrophages. One to two weeks after the bacteria were swallowed, they pour into the blood
again and a sustained fever begins. Diarrhoea is often absent. From the liver, bacteria pass in the
bile back into the gut, where the infected lymphoid patches can ulcerate, bleed or perforate.

This illness is **enteric fever**, a fever caused by *S.* Typhi, or by the related Paratyphi
serotypes, spreading from the gut through the lymph nodes, liver, spleen and blood. Enteric fever
caused by *S.* Typhi is **typhoid fever**. A small proportion of patients, more often those with
gallstones, go on to carry *S.* Typhi in the gallbladder for years, shedding it in their faeces
without being ill, and a carrier who prepares food can infect many people.

Humans are the only reservoir of *S.* Typhi, so safe water, sanitation and the treatment of carriers
could in principle eradicate it; non-typhoidal serotypes, which live in animals, cannot be eradicated
in this way (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain)).
Vaccines against typhoid, made from the capsular polysaccharide of *S.* Typhi, alone or linked to a
protein, or from live attenuated bacteria taken by mouth, are given to travellers and used where
typhoid is common (see [*Detecting and controlling
microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-prevent)). They protect only partly against
*S.* Typhi, and not reliably against the Paratyphi serotypes or the non-typhoidal serotypes.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Gastroenteritis | Non-typhoidal serotypes invade the lining of the end of the small intestine and the colon; neutrophils gather and the inflamed lining leaks fluid | Diarrhoea, fever and cramps in guests a day after a meal of undercooked chicken |
| Spread to the blood | Non-typhoidal bacteria that cross the gut lining reach the blood when the host's defences cannot contain them | Bacteraemia in an infant or an older adult after gastroenteritis |
| Enteric fever | *S.* Typhi survives inside macrophages, which carry it to the lymph nodes, liver, spleen and bone marrow, and then into the blood | A fever that rises day by day in a traveller back from South Asia |
| Chronic carriage | *S.* Typhi persists in the gallbladder, often on gallstones, and is shed in the faeces | A cook who feels well but is the source of an outbreak of typhoid |

Three conditions let *Salmonella* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | For gastroenteritis, anyone who swallows enough bacteria, with spread to the blood in infants, older adults and people with weakened defences; for typhoid, anyone without immunity where sanitation is poor, including travellers | Stomach acid kills many swallowed bacteria, so the inoculum matters; weaker defences fail to contain the bacteria that cross the gut lining |
| Where (setting) | For non-typhoidal serotypes, food from animals, especially poultry and eggs, left warm; for *S.* Typhi, food or water contaminated with human faeces | Non-typhoidal serotypes live in animals and multiply in warm food; *S.* Typhi lives only in humans, patients and carriers |
| How (route) | Swallowed; across the lining of the small intestine and into macrophages | It survives and multiplies inside macrophages, which carry it to the lymph nodes and the blood |

Step through the two routes *Salmonella* takes: non-typhoidal serotypes in the gut, and *S.* Typhi
through the whole body.

## Contrast pair {#sec-ent-pairs}

### *Salmonella* and *Shigella* {#sec-ent-pair-salmonella-shigella}

*Shigella* lives only in the human gut. It invades the cells lining the colon, kills them and spreads
from cell to cell, causing dysentery. Its **infectious dose**, the inoculum needed to cause infection,
is very small: as few as 10 to 100 *Shigella* bacteria can cause it, while non-typhoidal
*Salmonella* usually needs far more. Neither ferments lactose, so their colonies look alike on
MacConkey agar, and both are swallowed. Compare them feature by feature before reading the principle.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-salmonella-shigella.yml"></div>

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-ent-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-ent-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Shigella* | The human gut only | Does not ferment lactose and has no flagella; as few as 10 to 100 bacteria cause infection; invades the cells lining the colon and spreads from cell to cell; one serotype, *Shigella dysenteriae* type 1, makes Shiga toxin | Dysentery, spread from person to person in households and childcare centres, by sexual contact, and where sanitation is poor |
| *Proteus mirabilis* | The gut | Does not ferment lactose; spreads in a film across the surface of agar plates; makes **urease**, an enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide; the ammonia makes urine alkaline | Urinary tract infection, especially with a long-term urinary catheter; minerals crystallise from alkaline urine as stones, which shelter the bacteria and can block the catheter |
| *Yersinia enterocolitica* | The gut of pigs and other animals | Does not ferment lactose; grows at refrigerator temperatures, so it multiplies in chilled food | Diarrhoea and fever after undercooked pork or unpasteurised milk; in older children, inflamed lymph nodes beside the end of the small intestine, with pain that can be mistaken for appendicitis |

### Later in the course {#sec-ent-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *E. coli* | Renal medicine and urology (urinary tract infection); gastroenterology and paediatrics (diarrhoea and haemolytic uraemic syndrome); neonatology (meningitis and bloodstream infection); resistant strains in pharmacology |
| *K. pneumoniae* | Respiratory medicine and intensive care (pneumonia and bloodstream infection); hepatology (liver abscess); ophthalmology (endophthalmitis); infection control and pharmacology (carbapenem resistance) |
| *Salmonella* | Gastroenterology (gastroenteritis); infectious diseases and travel medicine (enteric fever); public health (food safety and carriers) |
| *Shigella* | Gastroenterology and paediatrics (dysentery) |
| *Proteus mirabilis* | Urology (urinary tract infection and stones) |
| *Yersinia enterocolitica* | Gastroenterology (diarrhoea, and pain that mimics appendicitis) |
